planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in average to sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; American barren strawberry is the native eastern North American counterpart to the more commonly sold Eurasian Waldsteinia ternata, and is preferred for native plant and pollinator-focused shade plantings.

directions: Plant divisions in average, well-drained, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; American barren strawberry is a low, mat-forming native perennial found naturally in dry to moist deciduous woods and rocky slopes from the Appalachians north into New England and the upper Midwest, spreading slowly by short rhizomes to form an evergreen to semi-evergreen carpet of glossy, three-lobed, strawberry-like leaves. Bright yellow, five-petaled flowers appear in mid-spring just above the foliage, followed by small dry seed heads rather than a fleshy fruit — despite the common name, it produces no edible berry. It is slower to spread and less aggressive than its Eurasian relative, making it a good choice for naturalizing under native hardwoods without overwhelming companion woodland wildflowers. Once established it needs little care and tolerates the dry, root-filled soil typical of a mature shade garden; supplemental water is only necessary during the first growing season or in prolonged drought.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Big Red Ripper Cowpea (Heirloom Dual-Purpose Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained soil in full sun; Big Red Ripper is a vigorous, sprawling vine that benefits from a trellis or ample row spacing, and can be sown successively through midsummer in zone 8–9.

directions: Direct sow in well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; Big Red Ripper is a heirloom Southern cowpea grown for its large, dark brownish-red seeds and rangy, vigorous vines that produce heavily even in poor, dry soil where other legumes struggle. It serves double duty as both a dry-shell eating pea, with a rich, earthy flavor good in soups and stews, and as a soil-building summer cover crop or wildlife food plot planting, since the sprawling vines fix nitrogen and suppress weeds while the abundant seed feeds deer, quail, and dove. Let pods dry fully on the vine for shell-bean storage, or harvest young green pods for fresh shelling if a more tender pea is preferred. Because vines ramble extensively, either trellis plants for easier picking or allow them to sprawl as a living mulch between wider-spaced garden rows. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it needs little irrigation through a Gulf Coast summer.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — heirloom cowpea variety notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Southern Pea Production
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Cowpea Plant Guide

common_name: Texas Cream 40 Pea (Extended-Harvest Cream Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is a semi-vining selection from the Texas A&M cream pea breeding series, bred to hold a longer, later harvest window than the more compact Texas Cream 8.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is part of the Texas A&M cream-type southern pea breeding series, selected for a longer, more extended pod set than the earlier-released Texas Cream 8, giving home gardeners a steadier trickle of pods for fresh picking rather than one concentrated flush. Seeds are creamy-white with the mild, delicate, slightly sweet flavor typical of cream peas, prized for fresh shelling and quick cooking. Plants are semi-vining and slightly more sprawling than Texas Cream 8, so allow a bit more row width or provide light support for easier picking. Pick pods while still slightly immature and the seeds are plump but not hardened for the best fresh-shell texture; pods left to fully dry make good storage peas as well. Consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill improves yield in the Gulf Coast heat of midsummer.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Southern Pea Variety Trials

common_name: Florida High Bush Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost at 80–85°F for germination; transplant into full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Florida High Bush grows into a tall, vigorous plant and benefits from staking once fruit load is heavy.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once the soil and nights are warm; Florida High Bush is an old Southern heirloom eggplant bred for reliable production through the intense heat and humidity of a Deep South summer, when many standard eggplant varieties stall or drop blossoms. Plants grow tall and vigorous — notably taller than most eggplant cultivars, as the name suggests — and bear a heavy, extended crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval to pear-shaped fruit with classic mild, creamy flesh. Because the bushes get large and top-heavy once loaded with fruit, stake or cage plants at transplanting to prevent wind and fruit-weight damage. Harvest fruit at about two-thirds of full size, while the skin is still glossy and taut — dull skin signals over-mature, seedier flesh. Regular harvesting encourages continued flowering and keeps plants productive from early summer through the first fall frost in zone 8–9.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — heirloom eggplant variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Production
Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom eggplant collection

common_name: Cherokee Long Ear Small Popcorn (Heirloom Native Popcorn)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 60°F in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plant in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure reliable wind pollination, and isolate from other corn varieties by at least several hundred feet to keep the strain true.

directions: Plant in blocks in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherokee Long Ear Small is a slender-eared heirloom popcorn preserved through Cherokee seed-saving tradition and maintained today by heritage seed savers, notable for its small stature and small, narrow ears carrying rows of hard, glossy kernels in mixed colors from white through red and blue. Plants are shorter and the ears smaller than modern hybrid popcorn, but the strain is valued for its resilience, drought tolerance, and the deep cultural history tied to Southeastern Native American foodways. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk until husks are papery and kernels are hard before harvesting; cure further indoors for several weeks in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing. Kernels pop reliably once fully cured, with a notably tender hull compared to many commercial popcorn hybrids. Save the best ears for the following year's seed to keep the strain vigorous and true.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom corn collection
Native Seeds/SEARCH — Southeastern heritage corn varieties
North Carolina State Extension — Sweet and Field Corn Production
